summaryEn: How do Joseon records help people today? Hoya sees a fortress repaired from uigwe drawings, a festival that recreates a royal procession, scientists reading old weather notes, and the Annals open to everyone online.
learningGoalsEn: Know at least two ways people use Joseon records today (restoring Hwaseong, recreating a procession, studying past weather, reading the Annals online).
Know that the Annals, Seungjeongwon Ilgi, Uigwe and Ilseongnok are all on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.
Read and recognize 기록은 보물이에요 (girogeun bomurieyo), 화성 (Hwaseong), 성 (seong), 행렬 (haengnyeol) and 날씨 (nalssi).

origin.noteEn: Heritage history, researched from the sources listed on the Sources screen.

scenes.narrationEn: Hoya has one more question: what do these old records do for us today? Let's visit some places where Joseon records are still at work.
scenes.captionEn: Hoya asks what old records do today
scenes.artBrief: Hoya with a small backpack standing at a crossroads with signposts shaped like a book, a fortress and a cloud (no text).

art.altEn: Hoya stands at a crossroads where a signpost points three ways, marked with a book, a fortress and a cloud.

scenes.narrationEn: Suwon Hwaseong Fortress was finished in 1796. Every step of the building work was recorded in the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe, with drawings of buildings and machines, and the sizes and amounts of materials.
scenes.captionEn: Hwaseong Fortress, recorded step by step
scenes.artBrief: A stone-and-brick fortress wall with a gate tower; beside it, an open book showing a drawing of a lifting machine with pulleys.

art.altEn: A gate of Hwaseong Fortress stands over its stone walls, beside an open book with a drawing of a pulley lifting machine.

scenes.narrationEn: Later, parts of the fortress were damaged. Workers followed the uigwe to restore it to its original shape, and repairs still rely on this record today.
scenes.captionEn: Repairing the fortress from the uigwe
scenes.artBrief: Modern workers in helmets fitting stones into a fortress wall while one checks a page of old drawings on a tablet.

art.altEn: Workers in hard hats fit a stone back into the fortress wall, checking the old uigwe drawings on a tablet.

scenes.narrationEn: Today, Suwon's Hwaseong Cultural Festival, the {kw:suwon-hwaseong-munhwaje}, includes a recreation of King Jeongjo's grand royal procession, based on the uigwe of his trip.
scenes.captionEn: A festival recreates the royal procession
scenes.artBrief: A modern street festival: people in colorful Joseon costumes marching with flags and a palanquin, families watching and waving.

art.altEn: At Suwon's festival today, people in Joseon costumes march with flags and a palanquin while families watch.

scenes.narrationEn: Scientists can study the daily weather notes in the Seungjeongwon Ilgi, which covers nearly 300 years, to learn about nature in the past.
scenes.captionEn: Scientists can study old weather notes

approximations.rationaleEn: The surviving diaries cover 288 years (1623-1910); narration rounds that to nearly 300.

scenes.artBrief: A scientist at a computer showing a simple line chart, with an old diary open on the desk and a window showing rain clouds.

art.altEn: A scientist studies a weather chart on a computer beside an old diary, with rain clouds outside the window.

scenes.narrationEn: The Annals were written in classical Chinese, which is hard for most people today. Translators turned them into modern Korean, and now anyone can read the translation online, along with the original text.
scenes.captionEn: Anyone can read the Annals online
scenes.artBrief: A child and a grandparent looking at a tablet showing two columns of text shapes, one old style and one modern (no readable characters).

art.altEn: A grandparent and a child read the Annals together on a tablet, the old text beside a modern translation.

scenes.narrationEn: All four records you met, the Annals, the Seungjeongwon Ilgi, the uigwe and the Ilseongnok, are on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.
scenes.captionEn: On UNESCO's Memory of the World

approximations.rationaleEn: f6 lists four records: the Annals, the Seungjeongwon Ilgi, the Uigwe and the Ilseongnok.

scenes.artBrief: Four old books standing side by side on a shelf with a soft glow, each a different cover color.

art.altEn: Four old books stand side by side: the Annals, the Royal Secretariat's diaries, the uigwe and the Ilseongnok.

scenes.narrationEn: Hoya smiles. Thanks to people who wrote carefully long ago, we can still learn from the past. 'Records are treasures!' What will you write down today?
scenes.artBrief: Hoya holding up a small notebook and brush, grinning, with the fortress, books and a sunny sky behind him.

art.altEn: Hoya cheers in front of the fortress and a stack of old books: records are treasures!

checks.promptEn: How was Suwon Hwaseong restored to its original shape?

options.en: By guessing from stories told by villagers
By copying a fortress from another country
By following the records and drawings in its uigwe

checks.promptEn: What can scientists study in the Seungjeongwon Ilgi?
checks.explainEn: The Seungjeongwon Ilgi recorded the weather every day, so scientists can use it to study nature in the past.

facts.claimEn: Suwon Hwaseong was completed in 1796, and the whole construction process was recorded in the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe, including architectural drawings, pictures of construction machines, and the sizes and quantities of materials.
facts.claimKo: 수원 화성은 1796년에 완성되었으며, 축성의 모든 과정이 건축 도면, 축성 기계 그림, 재료의 치수와 수량까지 『화성성역의궤』에 기록되었다.

verification.notes: Third independent pass. All Sillok entries (Taejong 4/2/8 #4; Jeongjo 19/leap2/13 #1 and #3) re-fetched from sillok.history.go.kr and compared to original Chinese/Korean text. Every non-UNESCO URL cited was re-fetched fresh and every quote segment machine-matched, plus heritage.go.kr 국가유산 설명 text loaded from the portal's own ajax file (DATA1/heritage/hub_img/html/cul_*.html). UNESCO register pages for all four items verified via Internet Archive (registration years 1997/2001/2007/2011 with exact wording); Uigwe nomination PDF re-extracted and quotes/section numbers verified; Seungjeongwon nomination PDF could not be re-fetched (captcha) so the author's saved text was used, with other sources backing each fact. Corrections this pass: poswae schedule mistranslation (격 2년 = every third year, not every other year), 'dried herbs' removed, ep5 f4 quote exactified, 3 vocab words not appearing in scenes removed, ep5 f8 second source (정병모 판화사적 연구) and ep6 f3 festival official site added, UNESCO locators replaced by exact page wording, ep3 f7 3,045+198 clarification.

authorNotes: The restoration years (1975-1979) appear in only one Korean source, so narration gives no year. Causes of the fortress damage (colonial period and Korean War) are omitted as out of scope; narration says only 'parts were damaged'. Festival: the official Korean name is 수원화성문화제 (the draft's '화성문화제' was the English-page rendering and the Encyclopedia headword); the claim is now backed by the KHS English page, the Suwon City page for the procession (which states it is based on the uigwe) and the Encyclopedia entry on the festival; 'every year in October' and any dates are left out of narration because the schedule can change (2026 events were held in early October). The translation completion year (1993) is single-source and omitted. Scenes 1 and 8 are story framing with no factual claims. UNESCO register pages are cited for registration years only (page wording not quoted; unesco.org was unreachable on 2026-10-10), and the NIKH list of Korean Memory of the World items is a second source for all four years. PASS 3: the festival-includes-procession link is now backed by the festival's own official site (63rd festival, 2026) in addition to the KHS English page and the Encyclopedia; Suwon City's tourism site lists the two as separate menu items, so the narration keeps the neutral 'includes'.
